newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU good for jobs - UNICE employers group.
newsitem.headline: EMU good for jobs - UNICE employers group.

text.p: Europe's planned monetary union will help boost the continent's competitiveness and lower high unemployment, according to the European employers' group UNICE.

"UNICE sees the move towards EMU as vital for the restoration of European competitiveness on which higher growth and job creation depend," the Union of Industrial and Employers' Confederation of Europe said in a statement.
"Contrary to some assertions, EMU should be seen not as part of the problem but as part of the solution to high levels of unemployment," it said.
The statement, made available to Reuters on Tuesday, called on European Union leaders meeting in Dublin on December 13 and 14 to keep on track for economic and monetary union.

It urged leaders to decide on a post-EMU budgetary stability pact, reinforced convergence procedures, a new exchange rate mechanism for EU currencies outside monetary union and a legal framework for the introduction of the euro.
"These decisions, which are vital for the credibility of EMU, must be taken strictly within the rules laid down by the existing treaty," it said.
Also, governments must allow companies to introduce the single currency at any time during the planned transition period, running from 1999 to 2002.
UNICE said monetary stability and sound financial policies would improve the business and investment environment in Europe, promoting growth without inflation and higher employment.

"Without EMU, maximum benefit will not be drawn from the single market, whose complete and effective implementation is the best way to bring about restructuring, deregulation and liberalisation of Europe's product, services and labour markets, so necessary to boost its competitiveness," it said.
UNICE also said the EU's intergovernmental conference (IGC), which is negotiating reform of the EU and its institutions, must avoid the ratification problems of the 1991 Maastricht treaty.

"Otherwise both EMU and the single market will be put at risk," it said, adding that the summit in Dublin should decide to limit the subjects under discussion to those essential for the effective functioning of the EU after enlargement.

"It should refuse discussion of issues unconnected with that objective and especially those which present a threat to competitiveness, to market liberalisation or to sound economcic and budgetary policies," the UNICE statement said.
